title: What to Practice on a Day You Do Not Feel Like Practicing
description: The days you do not feel like playing are the days that decide whether you are still playing in a year. Here is exactly what to do with them, and why ten minutes counts as a real session.
sub: Not a motivation lecture. One specific, small thing to do on the days when sitting down at the piano feels like too much.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: Forty-one lessons in order, free, so you never have to decide what to practice:
body:
Everyone who plays an instrument has these days. You know you should sit down. You do not want to. And the longer you stand in the doorway thinking about it, the larger the whole thing becomes.

What decides whether you are still playing in a year is not what you do on the good days. It is what you do on these ones.

Do not open the piece

On a low day, the worst thing you can do is open the piece you are working on. It is the hardest thing in your repertoire, it will go badly because you are tired, and you will finish the session holding fresh evidence that you are getting worse.

Leave it closed. The piece is not going anywhere.

The ten-minute version

Here is the whole instruction: sit down and play something you already know, slowly, for ten minutes.

Not to improve it. Not to fix anything. Play a piece you finished two months ago, at a comfortable speed, and listen to the sound. That is the entire session, and it is a complete one.

Three things happen. Your hands keep their habits, which is most of what practice is. You end on something that sounded good, so your association with the instrument stays warm. And you did not break the chain, which matters more than any single session’s content.

Why ten minutes is not a consolation prize

Adults treat a short session as a failed long one. It is not. The hand consolidates what it has learned between sessions rather than during them, which is why six ten-minute days beat one hour-long Sunday by a distance.

A ten-minute day is a real day. It is not half a session. It is a whole small one.

Three things worth doing when you have nothing in you

Play one scale, very slowly, and listen to the evenness. It asks almost nothing of your concentration and it works on the thing that is hardest to improve deliberately, which is tone.

Read something far below your level. A piece from the first weeks of the course. Reading improves with volume, and easy reading is the most pleasant volume there is.

Play the piece you started for. Everybody has one — the reason they sat down at a piano in the first place. Play it badly. It does not have to be a practice session to be worth the ten minutes.

The one thing not to do

Do not skip it and promise yourself a long session tomorrow. That trade is never honored, and it turns one missed day into a missed week, which is how most adults stop for good.

If you sit down for ten minutes on the bad days, you will still be playing next year. That is not motivation talking. It is the only reliable difference between the people who keep going and the people who do not.

title: How to Practice Slowly Without It Becoming Meaningless
description: Everyone is told to practice slowly and almost nobody is told how. Slow practice done wrong builds nothing. Here is what makes it work.
sub: “Practice it slowly” is the most-repeated advice in music and the least explained. There is a right way to do it, and most adults are not doing it.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko seated at the piano
cta_text: Every piece in the free course is demonstrated slowly first, then at tempo:
body:
Every teacher says it. Every book says it. Practice slowly. And then nobody explains what slow practice is for, so adults do the obvious thing — play the same notes at half speed while thinking about something else — and reasonably conclude it does not work.

It does work. But it is not the fast version played slower. It is a different activity.

What slow practice is actually doing

At speed, you cannot observe yourself. The notes arrive faster than attention can follow, so you play on autopilot and hear only the overall result — good or bad — with no information about why.

Slow practice buys you time between notes. In that time you can see where your hand is going next, notice a finger that is tightening, hear whether two notes were actually together. It is not an easier version of the piece. It is the version in which you can still perceive what you are doing.

Which leads straight to the rule that makes or breaks it.

If you are not noticing something, you are not practicing slowly

Slow playing with your attention elsewhere builds nothing. Worse, it builds nothing while feeling virtuous, which is why people do it for weeks and give up on the method.

So give each slow pass one job, out loud if it helps:

This pass I am watching the jump in bar 9.
This pass I am listening for whether the left-hand chord sounds as one sound.
This pass I am checking my shoulders.

One thing per pass. Three slow passes with a job each are worth more than twenty minutes of slow noise.

How slow is slow enough

Here is a test that removes the guesswork. Slow enough that you know the next note before you have to play it.

If you are reading each note at the instant your finger needs it, you are too fast, whatever the metronome says. When you can see ahead, you are at the right speed — and for a hard passage that is often absurdly slow, three or four times slower than the piece. That is fine. It is temporary.

Do not practice slowly with the pedal down

A small thing with a large effect. The sustain pedal covers gaps, so at slow speed it hides exactly the joins you are trying to inspect. Practice slow passages dry, then add the pedal back when the notes are secure.

Coming back up to speed

This is where the work is usually thrown away. People practice slowly for a week and then jump straight to full tempo, the passage falls apart, and they conclude slow practice does not transfer.

Come up in steps, and make each one boringly small — five or six clicks of the metronome at a time. At each new speed, play the passage twice correctly before you move up. If it breaks, go back two steps, not one.

The slowest speed you can play a passage badly is not your speed. The fastest speed at which it is still completely accurate is, and that number moves up on its own over days.

The short version

Slow enough to see ahead. One thing to notice per pass. No pedal. Come up in small steps and only from accuracy. Done that way, a passage that has resisted you for a month usually gives way in a week.

title: How Loud Is Loud? p, mf and f, Explained Practically
description: Dynamic markings are relative, not absolute, and almost nobody tells beginners that. Here is how to decide how loud your forte should actually be.
sub: There is no decibel value for forte. What there is, is a relationship — and once you see it, the markings stop being guesswork.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko in concert dress
cta_text: Dynamics arrive in their place in the free course, after the notes they shape:
body:
The letters under the staff are Italian abbreviations. p is piano, soft. f is forte, loud. mp and mf are mezzo — moderately — soft and loud. Add letters to go further: pp is very soft, ff very loud.

That much every method book says. What almost none of them say is the part that actually causes the trouble.

They are relative, not absolute

There is no volume that simply is forte. A forte in a quiet, slow piece is not the same sound as a forte in a big loud one. A forte on an upright in a small room is not a forte in a concert hall.

What the marking tells you is where this passage sits compared with the passage next to it. Dynamics are a landscape, not a measurement. The question is never “is this loud enough?” — it is “is this louder than the part before it, by roughly the amount the composer asked for?”

Read them that way and the anxiety goes out of them.

Find your own range first

Do this once, at your own instrument, and you will stop guessing.

Play a single note as softly as you can while still getting a clear sound — not a note that half-speaks, a real one. That is your floor. Now play one as loudly as you can without the tone turning harsh or the instrument banging. That is your ceiling. Listen to the distance between them.

Everything in every piece you play lives between those two sounds. mf is somewhere in the middle. p is near the floor but not on it. Your range is almost certainly wider than you have been using: most adult beginners spend their whole time in a narrow band around mezzo-forte, and the result sounds flat no matter how correct the notes are.

The mistake that makes forte sound bad

Loud is not the same as hard. The most common way an adult plays a forte is by striking from the fingers with a tightened wrist, and the sound comes out harsh and percussive. The piano complains.

Volume comes from arm weight, not finger force. Let more of the arm in behind the key, keep the wrist free, and the sound gets bigger while staying round. A big sound is a relaxed sound. That is counter-intuitive and it is true.

The mistake that makes piano sound bad

The opposite error: playing softly by pressing timidly, so some notes fail to speak at all and the line comes out with holes in it.

Soft still needs the key to go all the way down. Think of soft as controlled rather than weak — the hand stays in contact, the movement is small but definite. A quiet passage in which every note sounds is far more impressive than a loud one.

The twenty-second habit

Before you play a piece, look through it once and find the loudest marking and the softest one. Those two are the ends of your map. Everything else you play between them — and suddenly every marking in the middle has an obvious value.

That is the difference between playing dynamics and playing notes.

title: How to Start Sight-Reading: A Method You Can Begin This Week
description: Sight-reading is a separate skill from playing, it is trained differently, and most adults never train it at all. Here is the daily five minutes that builds it.
sub: You do not get better at reading by learning pieces. You get better by reading things you will never learn.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: Every lesson in the free course reads from the page, in order, from the first note:
body:
Here is something that surprises adults: the person who can play a difficult piece beautifully and the person who can sit down and read a new one are not necessarily the same person. They are two skills, trained two ways, and almost every self-taught adult trains only the first.

Learning a piece means reading a few bars and then repeating them until your hands know them. After a week you are not reading at all — you are remembering. That is fine, it is how pieces get learned, but it builds reading about as much as memorizing a paragraph builds literacy.

The rule that makes it work

Read things you will never learn. Five minutes a day, a piece you have not seen, played once, then never opened again.

That “never again” is the entire method. The moment you repeat it, you have stopped reading and started learning, and the exercise has quietly turned into something else.

Choose music far below your level

This is where adults sabotage themselves. Sight-reading material should be much easier than what you play — roughly two levels down. If you are working through the middle of a beginner course, read from its first weeks.

The aim is fluency, not challenge. You want the experience of the eye moving forward steadily while the hands keep up, because that is the thing being trained. A piece that stops you every two bars trains stopping.

The four rules of the five minutes

Look before you play. Ten seconds. What key, what time signature, what is the lowest and highest note, are there accidentals, does anything repeat? You are not reading the notes yet — you are getting the shape of the page.

Choose a tempo you can hold at the hardest bar. Find the busiest measure, imagine playing it, and set the speed from that. Nearly everyone starts too fast, because the first bar is easy.

Do not stop and do not go back. This is the rule that matters most. Wrong note — keep going. Missed bar — keep going. Stopping to correct is precisely the habit you are trying to break, and in real playing, going back is worse than a wrong note.

Do not look at your hands. You cannot read and watch at the same time. Feel for the keys. You will be surprised how much the hand already knows.

What improves, and when

For about two weeks it feels like nothing is happening. Then you notice you are seeing groups instead of single notes — a chord as a shape, a run as a direction. Then intervals stop being counted and start being recognized, which is the point at which reading speeds up sharply.

Five minutes a day. Not thirty minutes on Sunday: the skill is built by frequency, like vocabulary, and it fades quickly when you stop.

Where to find material

Anything below your level — the early pages of any beginner method, hymn books, easy folk-song collections, children’s albums by real composers. The public-domain libraries hold more free easy music than you could read in a decade.

One page a day, once each, never twice. That is the whole method, and in three months you will read things that stop you today.

title: What Is a Key Signature, and Why Does It Change?
description: Those sharps or flats at the start of every line are not decoration and not difficulty. They are an instruction that saves you reading hundreds of accidentals.
sub: A key signature is a labor-saving device. Understanding what it is doing makes it far less intimidating than it looks.
image_alt: The strings inside a grand piano
cta_text: Key signatures arrive after the scales they come from, in order, in the free course:
body:
At the start of every line of music, just after the clef, there may be a small group of sharps or flats. That is the key signature, and it says one thing: every note on these lines or spaces is sharp (or flat) for the whole piece, unless something tells you otherwise.

It is written once per line so that it does not have to be written hundreds of times inside the music. That is all it is — an abbreviation.

Where it comes from

A major scale is a fixed pattern of whole steps and half steps. Start that pattern on C and it uses only white keys, which is why C major has no sharps and no flats, and why nearly every beginner book starts there.

Start the same pattern on G and one note has to be raised to keep the pattern intact: F becomes F sharp. So the key of G major has one sharp — and rather than printing a sharp in front of every F in the piece, the key signature says it once.

Start on D and you need two. On A, three. Each new key adds one, always in the same order, which is why a key signature looks like an arbitrary cluster when it is actually a queue.

How to read one without memorizing anything

You do not need the circle of fifths to play a piece in G major. You need to know which notes are affected. Look at the key signature and name them — “there is a sharp on the F line, so every F is F sharp” — and then play.

Two habits make this reliable.

Say it out loud before you start. “One sharp: F sharp.” Three seconds, and it prevents the most common mistake in all of beginner reading, which is playing bar one correctly and forgetting by bar nine.

Circle the first two or three occurrences in pencil. Erase them once the hand has learned.

The natural sign, and why it appears

Sometimes a piece in a sharp key needs the plain white note anyway. That is what the natural sign does: it cancels the key signature for that one note, for the rest of that measure.

So a natural is not a new note to learn. It means “not this time” — and, like every accidental, the bar line clears it.

Why the key changes at all

Two reasons, both practical. Different keys sit differently under the hand: a piece can be far easier to play in one key than another because of where the black keys fall. And different keys have different colors — the same melody moved to another key does not sound identical, even to a listener who could not name what changed.

For now you only need the first half. The key signature is there to save ink and to tell you, once, which notes are not the plain white ones. Read it, say it, and play.

title: A Five-Minute Warm-Up That Is Actually Worth Doing
description: Most beginner warm-ups are finger exercises in disguise, and adults skip them for good reason. Here is a short one that genuinely prepares the hand.
sub: A warm-up is not practice and it is not an exercise. Its whole job is to get the hand and the ear ready, and that takes five minutes.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko seated at home
cta_text: The warm-up is taught in Lesson 1 of the free course, before any note:
body:
Adults skip the warm-up, and they are half right to. Most of what is printed under that heading is finger exercises — useful or not, but not a warm-up. An exercise asks the hand to work. A warm-up asks it to wake up.

The difference matters, because a cold hand grips, and a gripping hand cannot hear. The first ten minutes of your practice are worth roughly half as much when you start cold, so five minutes spent properly buys back more than it costs.

Before the keyboard: thirty seconds

Stand up. Let both arms hang at your sides, completely. Shake the hands loosely, as though flicking water off them, five or six times. Roll the shoulders back twice.

Then make tight fists and snap the fingers open, wide, five times. You are asking the small muscles to notice they exist.

Sit down and check the bench: forearms level with the keys or a little above, feet flat, elbows with room in front of you.

One: single notes, listening (one minute)

Play one note. Just one. Let the arm drop into it rather than pressing from the finger, and listen to the whole sound — the attack, and then the long decay after it.

Do that eight or ten times, moving up the keyboard, alternating hands. It sounds like nothing and it does two things at once: it sets the arm weight for the session, and it turns your ear on before your fingers get busy.

Two: five notes, very slowly (two minutes)

Right hand thumb on C, one finger per key: C D E F G and back down. Slowly. What you are listening for is evenness — are all five notes the same weight? Most people have one finger that speaks louder (usually the thumb) and one that fades (usually the fourth).

Then the same with the left hand. Then, if you are comfortable hands together, both.

Do not speed it up. Speed is not the point, and this is not an exercise — you are checking that the hand does what you ask it to.

Three: something you know (a minute and a half)

Play a few bars of a piece you finished weeks ago, easily, at a comfortable tempo. It moves the hand into real music rather than patterns, and it puts you in a good mood, which is a legitimate goal.

The check that ends it

One last thing, and it takes five seconds. Put your hands in your lap and notice your shoulders. If they are up near your ears — and after a working day they usually are — drop them, breathe out, and begin.

Five minutes. No exercise book, nothing to buy, nothing to get better at. The hand is warm, the ear is on, the shoulders are down, and the practice that follows is worth more than it would have been.

title: Finger Independence: What Helps, and What Quietly Causes Injury
description: The fourth finger will never be as free as the others — that is anatomy, not weakness. Here is what can genuinely be trained, and which famous exercises to avoid.
sub: Some of the best-known finger exercises in piano history have injured more hands than they have helped. The anatomy explains why.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko in concert dress
cta_text: Technique is taught inside real music in the free course, not as separate drills:
body:
Every adult beginner meets the fourth finger and concludes something is wrong with their hand. It will not lift as far. It drags the third along with it. On its own it feels half-asleep.

Nothing is wrong. The fourth finger shares its tendon arrangement with its neighbors in a way the others do not, and no amount of training separates them completely. Look at any concert pianist’s hand and the fourth finger is doing the same thing. They have simply stopped asking it to do what it cannot.

What can actually be trained

Evenness of sound, not equality of movement. The goal was never five identical fingers. It is five notes that sound the same. A weaker finger is compensated by the hand and arm behind it, and that compensation is much of what technique is.

Timing. You can absolutely train a finger to arrive when you intend it to, and that is most of what “independence” means in practice.

Releasing. Beginners concentrate on pressing. Half of clean playing is letting go on time, and that is trainable in every finger.

The exercise worth doing

Play five notes — C D E F G — slowly, one finger per key, listening to nothing except whether all five sound the same weight. When one is louder or softer, do not press harder with the weak one. Instead let the hand lean very slightly toward it, so the arm supplies what the finger cannot.

That single habit does more for evenness than any drill, and it builds the right reflex: the arm helps the finger; the finger does not fight alone.

The famous exercises to be careful with

There is a nineteenth-century tradition of exercises that hold some fingers down while others lift, forcing the weak ones to work in isolation. They are still printed and still recommended.

They are also the most reliable way an amateur hurts themselves. Holding keys down while straining others loads exactly the structures that cannot take it, for long stretches, with no music to tell you when to stop. The history of the instrument includes a famous case of a hand ruined this way, and a great many unfamous ones.

If an exercise asks you to hold fingers down while lifting others against resistance, skip it. There is nothing in it you cannot get more safely elsewhere.

The rule that keeps you safe

Nothing should ever hurt, and nothing should ever be held tight. Not ache, not burn, not “work through it.” Mild fatigue in the forearm after half an hour is ordinary; pain in the hand, wrist or fingers is a signal to stop for the day.

Practice technique inside real music, in short spells, with the arm involved and the wrist free. The fourth finger will still be the fourth finger in ten years. Your playing will not sound like it.

title: Reading Ledger Lines Without Counting Every Time
description: Notes above and below the staff stop most adult readers cold. There is a way to read them by landmark instead of counting up from the last line.
sub: Those little extra lines are not a new alphabet. Two landmarks and one habit turn them into notes you recognize.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: The staff is built up landmark by landmark from Lesson 3 of the free course:
body:
A staff has five lines. Music does not stop at the top or the bottom of them, so when a note goes higher or lower, a short line is drawn just for that note. That short line is a ledger line, and you can stack several of them.

They are the point at which most adult reading slows to a crawl, because the usual method is to count — top line F, space above G, first ledger line A — every single time, for every single note.

Counting works. It is just far too slow to read with, and it does not get faster with repetition, because counting is not recognition.

Start from the one you already know

You already read one ledger line fluently and have done since your first week: middle C, on its own short line below the treble staff and above the bass staff. You do not count to it. You see it.

That is the proof that ledger lines can be recognized rather than computed. It is also the first landmark.

The landmarks worth learning

Instead of learning every ledger note, learn four fixed points and read the neighbors from them.

Middle C — one ledger line below the treble staff; one ledger line above the bass staff. The pivot of the whole grand staff.

The A just above the treble staff — the first ledger line up. Very common, worth knowing on sight.

High C — two ledger lines above the treble staff. It is an octave above the top-line F’s neighborhood and it is the ceiling of most beginner music.

The E two ledger lines below the bass staff — the low landmark, an octave below the bottom line G’s neighborhood.

Anything else you meet is one step above or below one of those four, and one step is instant, where counting five is not.

Read the interval, not the note

The faster habit, and the one real readers use: do not identify a high ledger note at all. Identify its distance from the note before it.

If the previous note was the top-line F and the next one is two spaces higher, your hand moves that distance, and it does not matter in the moment what the note is called. Reading by interval is what makes fast passages possible, and it works above the staff exactly as it works inside it.

The five minutes that fixes it

Write out, once, the four landmarks above — on paper, by hand. Then for a week, before you practice, find each of them on the keyboard and play it. Thirty seconds a day.

Then read easy music that uses them. Hymn books and simple arrangements are full of ledger lines and gentle in every other respect, which is exactly what you want: hard in the one dimension you are training and easy in all the rest.

A week of that and the counting stops. It does not fade gradually — one day you simply see A instead of counting to it.

title: Why You Cannot Play Fast Yet (It Is Not Your Fingers)
description: Speed at the piano is not a muscular limit for almost any adult. It is one of four specific things, and three of them are fixable this month.
sub: Adults assume speed comes with strength or youth. It comes from efficiency of movement, and here is what is eating yours.
image_alt: The strings and hammers inside a grand piano
cta_text: The free course builds speed the way it is actually built — from accuracy, in order:
body:
You can play the passage. You cannot play it at the speed it is meant to go. Push the tempo and it collapses in the same place every time.

Nearly every adult concludes their fingers are too slow, or too old, or not strong enough. That is almost never what is happening. Piano keys need very little force, and the finger movements involved are small and quick for essentially every adult hand. Something else is costing you the time, and it is usually one of four things.

1. You are still deciding

The most common cause by far. At slow speed you have time to work out the next note, the next fingering, the next hand position — and you are doing exactly that, invisibly, every time you play it.

Speed removes that time. If any part of the passage is still being decided rather than known, that is where it breaks.

The test: can you play the passage while saying something out loud — counting, or naming the beats? If your speech stops where the passage falters, you were thinking, not playing.

The fix: fix the fingering in writing and never change it again, and practice the passage until it survives that talking test. Speed usually arrives on its own afterward.

2. You are lifting too far

Watch your fingers in a fast passage. If they rise well clear of the keys between notes, every note is a round trip — up and back down — and at speed there is no time for the journey.

Fast playing happens close to the keys. The finger stays near the surface and the movement is small. This feels unnatural at first because high lifting feels like effort, and effort feels like work.

The fix: practice the passage at medium speed with the fingers deliberately touching the key surface between notes. It will feel lazy. It is the correct motion.

3. You are holding on

Tension is the real speed limit. A hand that is gripping has to overcome itself for every note, and fast passages are where that tax becomes unpayable.

Check the usual suspects: shoulders up, elbows clamped to the ribs, thumb pressing into the key it is not playing, jaw tight, breath held. Any one of them will cap your tempo.

The fix: play the passage at half speed, and once per bar deliberately release — drop the shoulders, let the wrist float, exhale. You are training the hand to stay loose at speed, and it has to learn that slowly.

4. You practiced it fast too early

If you have been playing it fast and messy for weeks, you have been rehearsing the mess. The hand learned a version of the passage that includes the stumble, and now the stumble is part of what it knows.

The fix is the only slow one here. Take it right back to a speed at which it is completely clean, live there for a few days, and come up in small steps from accuracy rather than from ambition.

The one that is not on the list

Finger strength. Building it will not increase your speed, and the exercises sold for it tend to add tension, which reduces it. Speed is an efficiency problem, not a power problem — which is good news, because efficiency is trainable at any age.

title: Andante, Allegro, Moderato: What Tempo Markings Actually Mean
description: The Italian word at the top of the page is not a speed you must hit. It is a character, and reading it that way changes how the piece sounds.
sub: Beginners look up Allegro, find a number, and set the metronome. That is not quite what the word is for.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko seated at the piano
cta_text: Tempo is taught as character, not as a number, throughout the free course:
body:
At the top of the music, above the first bar, there is usually an Italian word. It tells you how fast — roughly — and, more usefully, what kind of piece this is.

From slowest to fastest, the ones you will actually meet:

Largo — broad, very slow.
Adagio — slow, at ease.
Andante — literally “walking.” A comfortable walking pace.
Moderato — moderate.
Allegro — the word means cheerful, not fast. Quick and bright.
Vivace — lively.
Presto — very fast.

Why the words are not numbers

Look up Allegro and you will find something like 120 to 168 beats per minute. That range is enormous — the top end is nearly half again as fast as the bottom — and that is not sloppiness. It is the point.

Allegro in a light two-page piece is not Allegro in a dense one with chords in both hands. The music itself decides where in the range it sits. The word tells you the character; the notes tell you the speed.

Notice how many of the words are descriptions of mood or motion rather than velocity. Andante is a walk. Allegro is cheerful. Largo is broad. Composers were describing how a piece behaves, and the tempo follows from that.

The modifiers

A few small words do most of the adjusting:

molto — very. poco — a little. non troppo — not too much. ma non troppo — but not too much. assai — quite.

So Allegro ma non troppo is “quick, but do not overdo it,” which is a composer’s way of saying: this will be tempting to rush, and it should not be rushed.

Changing speed inside a piece

Three you will see constantly, usually abbreviated:

rit. (ritardando) — gradually slowing.
accel. (accelerando) — gradually getting faster.
a tempo — back to the original speed, after one of the above.

And rubato, which means the pulse is allowed to stretch and recover expressively — a subject of its own, and best left until the piece is secure in strict time.

The practical part

Adults do two things with tempo markings and both cause trouble.

They set the metronome to the top of the range and try to get there. Then the piece is learned in a panic and never sounds settled. Choose the speed at which the hardest bar is comfortable, and let that be the tempo. A clean Andante is worth far more than a frantic Allegro.

They ignore the word entirely and play everything at one speed. The word is the first piece of information the composer gives you about what this music is. Read it before the first note, decide what kind of piece it is going to be, and start from there.

“Walking” is a real instruction. Played as one, an Andante immediately sounds like music instead of notes.

title: Arpeggios: What They Are and Why They Feel Impossible at First
description: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time. The difficulty is not the notes — it is a single movement nobody explains, and it can be learned in a week.
sub: If arpeggios feel lumpy and uneven no matter how slowly you go, you are almost certainly missing one specific motion.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: Chords come before arpeggios in the free course, in that order and for a reason:
body:
An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time instead of all together. The word comes from the Italian for harp, because that is what a harp does with a chord.

Play C, E and G at once and you have a C major chord. Play C, then E, then G, one after the other, and you have arpeggiated it. Same three notes, spread out in time. That is the whole definition, and it explains why arpeggios turn up everywhere in real music: they are how the left hand keeps harmony going underneath a melody without drowning it.

Why they are harder than they look

Three notes, all of them known, in a shape you can already play as a block chord. And yet the arpeggio comes out lumpy, uneven, with a bump in the middle.

The reason is that an arpeggio spans more keyboard than your hand does. A chord sits under a fixed hand. An arpeggio, as soon as it goes past five notes, requires the hand to move along the keyboard while it is playing — and that motion, the thumb passing under, is the whole difficulty.

The movement nobody explains

Here is what most adults do: they keep the hand in one place and stretch the thumb sideways to reach the next note. The stretch creates tension, the tension creates the bump, and the bump never goes away no matter how slowly they play.

What should happen instead: the elbow and forearm travel with the hand. The thumb is not reaching anywhere. The whole arm moves a few inches along the keyboard, carrying the hand into position, and the thumb simply arrives where it needs to be.

And a small thing that makes it possible: as the thumb passes under, let the wrist rise very slightly and the elbow ease out from your side. That clears the road. A locked elbow forces the thumb to do a job it cannot do.

How to practice one

Play it as a block first. C E G together, then move the hand up and play the next C E G together. Get the shape and the jump secure with no melody to think about.

Then break it. Same notes, one at a time, at a speed where you can watch the arm move.

Then listen for the bump. There is always one note that is louder or late — almost always the thumb after it passes under. Play just those two notes, over and over, until they are equal.

Then join it up, slowly, listening for evenness rather than speed.

How long it takes

Less time than you expect, once the arm is involved. The reason arpeggios feel impossible is almost never the notes — it is a stretched thumb and a stationary elbow, and both of those are habits rather than limitations.

A week of five minutes a day, with the arm traveling, and the lumps go out of them.

title: When Should You Move On From a Piece?
description: Adults keep pieces far too long, waiting for a perfection that will not arrive. Here are four honest signs it is time, and one good reason to stay.
sub: You do not have to finish a piece to have learned from it. Knowing when to let one go is a skill of its own.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko seated at home
cta_text: The free course moves in order, so you always know what comes next:
body:
Adults working alone almost always keep a piece too long. There is no teacher to say “good, take this next,” so the piece stays open for months, gradually stops improving, and quietly turns into the reason practice has become dull.

The opposite error exists too — abandoning everything at the halfway point and never finishing anything — but it is much less common in adults, who tend to be conscientious to their own cost.

The honest test

Ask one question: has this piece improved in the last two weeks?

Not “is it perfect.” Not “could it be better” — everything could be better. Has it actually moved in fourteen days of practice?

If it has not, the piece has taught you what it has to teach. Keeping it open past that point is repetition, not learning.

Four signs it is time

You can play it through at tempo with the right notes, and the mistakes that remain are different every time. Random mistakes are a concentration matter, not a learning one, and they do not respond to more repetition.

You are bored of it. This is a legitimate reason and adults dismiss it as laziness. It is not: a bored player stops listening, and practice without listening does nothing.

The remaining problem is a skill the piece cannot teach you. If the only thing standing between you and a clean performance is, say, pedaling you have never been shown, the piece cannot fix that. Go and learn the skill, then come back.

You are only still playing it because you have not chosen the next one. Very common, and easily solved: choose the next one.

One good reason to stay

If it is still improving, stay. A piece you can play from memory, musically, at tempo is worth far more than four pieces you half-know — and finishing something all the way through is a distinct experience that teaches you what “finished” feels like. If you have never had that with any piece, have it with this one.

Leaving is not losing it

The part adults do not expect: a piece keeps improving after you put it down. Set it aside for two months, come back, and it is often better than when you left — the awkward passages have loosened and the whole thing sits more easily under the hand.

So moving on is not abandonment. Put it in a short list of pieces to revisit, take something new, and open it again in the spring. It will feel like meeting someone you know well.

And keep the finished ones

Play the pieces you have finished, regularly, for no reason other than that you can. It is the warm-up on tired days, it is what you play when somebody asks, and it is the clearest evidence you have that the work is going somewhere.

title: Repeat Signs, D.C., Coda: How to Find Your Way Through a Piece
description: The symbols that tell you where to go next confuse more beginners than the notes do. Here is the whole road map in one page.
sub: Da capo, dal segno, the coda sign, first and second endings — these are directions, not music, and they are simpler than they look.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko in concert dress
cta_text: The free course reads from real scores, with every marking explained as it appears:
body:
You can read every note on the page and still get lost, because printed music contains a second layer of instructions that has nothing to do with pitch or rhythm. It tells you the order to play things in.

Music is repetitive by nature, and rather than print the same sixteen bars three times, publishers use a handful of symbols meaning “go back there.” Here is the entire vocabulary.

Repeat bars

A double bar line with two dots before it means: go back and play that section again.

Back to where? To the matching sign with the dots facing the other way. If there is no such sign, back to the very beginning. That is the most common case and the one that catches people out — a single repeat sign late in the page can send you all the way to bar one.

First and second endings

Brackets over the last bars of a repeated section, numbered 1 and 2.

Play through the section including the bar under bracket 1, take the repeat, and the second time through skip the bar under bracket 1 entirely and play the one under bracket 2 instead. Then carry on.

The purpose is ordinary: the section needs one ending to lead back round again, and a different one to move forward.

D.C. and D.S.

D.C. is da capo — “from the head.” Go back to the beginning.

D.S. is dal segno — “from the sign.” Go back to the segno, an ornamented S with a slash and two dots, printed somewhere earlier in the piece. Find it first, before you start playing, or you will be hunting for it at speed.

al Fine added to either means: go back, then play until the word Fine and stop there. The piece ends in the middle of the page, which looks wrong the first time and is correct.

The coda

al Coda means: go back, play forward until you see the coda sign (a circle with a cross through it), then jump to the matching coda sign near the end and play the closing section.

So D.S. al Coda reads: back to the segno, forward to the coda mark, jump to the coda, finish. Three instructions in four characters, which is why it looks like cryptography until you have unpacked it once.

The habit that solves all of this

Trace the route before you play a note. Take a pencil and number the sections in the order you will actually play them — 1, 2, 3 — writing the numbers straight onto the score. Put an arrow where each jump goes.

Thirty seconds, once, and you will never get lost in that piece again. Professional musicians do exactly this, in pencil, on their own copies, and their scores are covered in arrows.

Getting lost in a piece is not a reading failure. It is navigation, and navigators use maps.
